page_hint: Ch 13 §3 'Placing the Canonical Workload'; Table 13-1; Fig 13.1 caption; Ch 13 §8 mini-case
quoted_clause: "the canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload sits on the **server** tier as a *fleet* of ~21 server-class hosts at the 40 rps peak ... the traffic scaling is a **cluster** of server-class hosts"; "So the **server** tier is the right *model-residency* archetype"; Table 13-1: "Cluster | tens-hundreds | ... | model > node, or traffic > host goodput"; Fig 13.1 caption: "Multi-host = Cluster"; mini-case: "the architect climbed the ladder precisely one rung"
observed: The chapter simultaneously places the canonical 21-host fleet on the 'server tier' and calls the same fleet a 'cluster of server-class hosts'. Table 13-1 and Fig 13.1's rung mapping (Multi-host = Cluster) place any multi-host deployment on the Cluster rung, so the canonical workload is already on the cluster rung by the chapter's own figure. The mini-case then claims the architect 'climbed the ladder precisely one rung' from server to cluster, which contradicts §3's placement of the canonical workload on the multi-host rung.
correction: Separate the two axes explicitly and use one term per axis — e.g. 'server-class hardware' (form factor) and 'cluster deployment' (scale) — and restate the canonical placement as 'server-class hardware, cluster deployment (21 hosts at the 40 rps peak)'. Restate the mini-case's climb as 'from single-host to multi-host deployment' rather than 'one rung', and make Table 13-1 and Fig 13.1's rung labels consistent with the prose.
acceptance_test: Ch 13 uses a single consistent term for each axis; the canonical workload's placement and the mini-case's escalation are stated in those terms and do not conflict; Table 13-1's 'When to use' column and Fig 13.1's rung mapping agree with the prose.
verdict_evidence: chapter-13.md:40 places the workload 'on the **server** tier as a *fleet* of ~21 server-class hosts ... the traffic scaling is a **cluster** of server-class hosts', while Table 13-1 (:68) defines Cluster as 'multiple hosts ... model > node, or traffic > host goodput' and Fig 13.1 (:95) maps 'Multi-host = Cluster'; the mini-case (:108) then calls the escalation 'precisely one rung'.
fix_instruction: Separate form factor from deployment scale in Ch 13: restate :40 as 'server-class hardware, cluster deployment (~21 hosts at the 40 rps peak)', and restate the mini-case's climb as 'from single-host to multi-host deployment' so Table 13-1, Fig 13.1 and the prose agree.

page_hint: Ch 13 §3 subsection heading 'Dropping a Tier: When Privacy Forces Local'; Ch 13 §5 Common Mistakes; Fig 13.1 caption
quoted_clause: Heading: "### Dropping a Tier: When Privacy Forces Local"; body: "privacy alone forces the on-prem **server** tier (data stays in the facility; the canonical 70B still runs on server hardware)"; Common Mistakes: "Privacy/geography can force a *lower* tier regardless of what compute wants"; Fig 13.1 caption: "de-escalation (blue) fires on privacy, sovereignty, and cost"
observed: Three places (the subsection heading, the common-mistake bullet, and the figure caption) treat privacy as a trigger to move *down* to the local/edge tier, while the subsection's own body says privacy forces the on-prem *server* tier and that local/edge applies only when the model can be distilled *and* must run on-device. 'Data must stay in the facility' and 'inference must run on the device' are different constraints with different tier consequences; the chapter conflates them.
correction: Split the constraint into two named constraints — data residency/sovereignty → on-prem server or cluster; on-device/offline/connectivity → local/edge — retitle the subsection accordingly (e.g. 'When On-Device Execution Forces Local'), and correct the common-mistake bullet and Fig 13.1's caption so each names the specific constraint it refers to.
acceptance_test: No text in Ch 13 asserts that privacy alone forces the local/edge tier; the subsection title, the common-mistake bullet and Fig 13.1's caption each name the specific constraint they refer to; the mini-case's 'data privacy requirement still forbids a public hyperscale cloud' is consistent with the same distinction.
verdict_evidence: Heading chapter-13.md:58 says 'Dropping a Tier: When Privacy Forces Local', but the body (:60) says 'privacy alone forces the on-prem **server** tier ... The **local/edge** tier applies only when the model can be distilled to a 7-13B ... *and* must run on-device'; the heading asserts a conclusion the body rejects.
fix_instruction: Retitle chapter-13.md:58 to 'Dropping a Tier: When On-Device Execution Forces Local' and split the two constraints in :60 (data residency -> on-prem server/cluster; offline/on-device -> local/edge).

page_hint: Ch 13 §3 'Escalating: When 10×Traffic Forces the Cluster Tier' vs Ch 13 §8 mini-case
quoted_clause: §3: "⌈100 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = ⌈50.59⌉ = **51 hosts at full utilization**, and Ch17's 70% utilization target plus the N−1 spare gives 73 working + 1 spare = **74 hosts** ... 77 working + 1 spare = **78 hosts** at the Table 17-1 policy"; mini-case: "the fleet is ⌈100 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = **51 hosts at full utilization** — 73 working + 1 spare = **74 hosts** ... or 77 working + 1 spare = **78 hosts** at the Table 17-1 policy"
observed: The mini-case reproduces §3's escalation arithmetic verbatim — same screen, same numbers, same intermediate quotients — and adds only the privacy constraint and a TTFT figure. The mini-case therefore does not require the reader to apply the chapter's reasoning to a decision the worked example has already made for them; it is a restatement, not a case.
correction: Give the mini-case a genuine twist that the ladder must resolve — e.g. a workload whose peak/average shape differs from the canonical 4×, a privacy constraint that forbids the cluster tier, or a model that no longer fits one node — and require the reader to compute the resulting tier and fleet from the chapter's triggers.
acceptance_test: The mini-case contains at least one quantity or decision not already computed in §3, and its answer either differs from or qualifies §3's conclusion.
verdict_evidence: chapter-13.md §3 'Escalating': 'At ~100 rps × 9.5K tokens = ~950K tokens/s, one host's goodput is exceeded' mixes the total-token basis (9.2K input + 300 output = 9.5K) with the input-token basis used everywhere else in the chapter and book for prefill screens (Ch 12: '~92K input tokens/s average and ~368K input tokens/s peak', so 100 rps = 920K input tokens/s, not 950K); the subsequent host count uses a different screen entirely ('⌈100 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = 51 hosts').
fix_instruction: In Ch 13 §3, state the basis explicitly — e.g. '~920K input tokens/s (100 rps × 9.2K input; ~950K total tokens including the 300 output tokens), far above one host's ~19.8K prefill ceiling' — and note that the host count that follows comes from the KV/service-time screen, not a tokens/s comparison.

page_hint: Ch 13 §3 'Placing the Canonical Workload' and 'Escalating' subsections
quoted_clause: "under the 70% × 95% policy — applied to the unrounded 344/17 ≈ 20.2, not the rounded 21 — that becomes 31 working + 1 spare = 32 total"; "on the ρ = 1 u-only screen — 77 working + 1 spare = **78 hosts** at the Table 17-1 policy (u × ρ = 0.665; ⌈860/11.305⌉ = ⌈76.07⌉ = 77)"
observed: The symbols u and ρ are used without definition anywhere in the chapter. From the arithmetic, u = 0.70 (utilization target) and ρ = 0.95 (the second policy factor), with 'ρ = 1 u-only screen' meaning the 0.95 factor is omitted; but 'u × ρ = 0.665' with ρ = 1 would give u = 0.665, so the notation is internally ambiguous as written. 11.305 = 17 × 0.665 is also unexplained.
correction: Define u and ρ at first use in Ch 13 (e.g. 'u = 0.70 utilization target, ρ = 0.95 peak headroom factor, per Ch 17's Table 17-1 policy') or cross-reference the definition explicitly.
acceptance_test: Every symbol used in Ch 13's host-count arithmetic is defined in Ch 13 or explicitly cross-referenced to its definition.
verdict_evidence: chapter-13.md:44 and :56 use 'u', 'ρ' and 'u x ρ = 0.665' with no local definition; they are defined only in chapter-17.md:105/114 (u = 0.70 utilization target, ρ = 0.95 LB efficiency). Arithmetic checks: 17 x 0.665 = 11.305, 860/11.305 = 76.07, 50.59/0.70 = 72.3 -> 73.
fix_instruction: Define the symbols at first use in chapter-13.md:44 (e.g. 'u = 0.70 utilization target, rho = 0.95 load-balancer efficiency, per Ch 17 Table 17-1') and use one notation for the 74-host rho = 1 case.

quoted_clause: "The naive ~100 ÷ 2.0 ≈ 50 understates the fleet: the ~2.0 rps screen uses the unfloored 17.5-slot quotient and applies no utilization headroom, so 50 hosts could only deliver 50 × 17/8.6 ≈ 98.8 rps — below demand."
observed: The framing implies the naive screen is materially wrong, but the naive screen (50) and the corrected full-utilization screen (51) differ by one host; the material difference (74 or 78 hosts) comes from the utilization headroom and N−1 rule, not from the slot flooring. As written, the reader is invited to attribute the fleet size to the flooring choice.
correction: Reword so the one-host difference is attributed to slot flooring and the 50 → 74/78 difference is attributed to the utilization headroom and N−1 policy.
acceptance_test: The paragraph's attribution of each difference (flooring vs headroom) matches the arithmetic.
verdict_evidence: chapter-13.md:56 says the naive '100 / 2.0 ~ 50 understates the fleet ... so 50 hosts could only deliver 50 x 17/8.6 ~ 98.8 rps', but 50 vs ceil(50.59) = 51 is a one-host flooring difference, and the 74/78 figures come entirely from the 0.70/0.665 headroom plus N-1; the 'so' clause attributes the gap to the wrong cause (and headroom cannot explain 98.8 rps, which is a full-utilization rate).
fix_instruction: Reword chapter-13.md:56: 'the naive screen is one host short (50 vs ceil(50.59) = 51) because it uses the unfloored 17.5-slot quotient; the larger 50 -> 74/78 gap comes from the 70% x 95% headroom and the N-1 spare.'

quoted_clause: The canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload sits on the server tier as a fleet of ~21 server-class hosts at the 40 rps peak
observed: Table 13-1 defines 'Server' as one host with 1–8 GPUs and 'Cluster' as multiple hosts (tens to hundreds of GPUs). A fleet of ~21 hosts is a cluster by that definition. The sentence tries to distinguish 'server-class model residency' from 'cluster-tier deployment,' but it uses 'server tier' for the deployment, which contradicts the table.
correction: Rewrite the first sentence as: 'The canonical workload's model residency is server-class, but its deployment at the 40 rps peak is a cluster of ~21 server-class hosts.' Then use 'server-class residency' and 'cluster-tier deployment' consistently in §13.3 and §13.6.
acceptance_test: The tier label in §13.3 matches Table 13-1's definition: one host = Server; multiple hosts = Cluster. A reader cannot conclude that a 21-host fleet is a single server-tier deployment.
verdict_evidence: Ch13 §3: "The canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload sits on the server tier as a fleet of ~21 server-class hosts" while Table 13-1 defines Server as 1-8 GPUs and Cluster as "tens-hundreds"; 21 hosts x 8 = 168 GPUs is a Cluster by that table, and the same sentence already says the scaling "is a cluster of server-class hosts".
fix_instruction: Change the opening clause to "The canonical workload's model residency is server-class, and at the 40 rps peak its deployment is a cluster of ~21 server-class hosts", keeping the rest of the sentence unchanged.

quoted_clause: Latency/geography: SLO can't be met due to distance or contention → split prefill/decode (a within-tier move).
observed: P/D disaggregation addresses phase contention and mismatched resource binding, not network distance or geography. Distance is a placement problem (edge/region/local), not a P/D problem.
correction: Split the trigger: "contention/phase interference → P/D disaggregation" and "distance/geography → placement to a lower or different tier, or regional replicas".
acceptance_test: A reader should map distance to placement, not to P/D disaggregation.
verdict_evidence: The escalation bullet reads '**Latency/geography**: SLO can't be met due to distance or contention → split prefill/decode (a within-tier move)', yet the same paragraph assigns distance to placement: 'moving the serving edge closer (local) is a placement move to a lower rung, not a climb trigger'. P/D splits phases; it does not shorten a network path.
fix_instruction: Split the trigger: 'contention/phase interference → split prefill/decode (a within-tier move)' and 'distance/geography → move the serving edge closer or add regional replicas (a placement move, not a climb)'.

page_hint: Chapter 13, §3 Worked Example, Escalating: When 10×Traffic Forces the Cluster Tier
quoted_clause: the ~2.0 rps screen uses the unfloored 17.5-slot quotient and applies no utilization headroom, so 50 hosts could only deliver 50 × 17/8.6 ≈ 98.8 rps — below demand.
observed: The sentence says the screen uses the unfloored 17.5-slot quotient, but the calculation uses the floored 17 slots. With 17.5 slots, 50 hosts deliver 50 × 17.5 / 8.6 ≈ 101.7 rps, not 98.8 rps.
correction: State both clearly: using the conservative floored 17 slots, 50 hosts deliver 98.8 rps; using 17.5 slots, they deliver ~101.7 rps but with no utilization headroom and based on a rounded 2.0 rps figure.
acceptance_test: The slot count used in the arithmetic must match the slot count named in the sentence.
verdict_evidence: ch13: 'the ~2.0 rps screen uses the unfloored 17.5-slot quotient ..., so 50 hosts could only deliver 50 × 17/8.6 ≈ 98.8 rps' — the label says 17.5 but the arithmetic uses 17. 50 × 17.5/8.6 ≈ 101.7 rps; 50 × 17/8.6 ≈ 98.8 rps, and 101.7 > 100 rps demand.
fix_instruction: State the screen honestly: 'the ~2.0 rps screen (17.5 slots ÷ 8.6 s ≈ 2.03 rps/host) gives 50 × 2.03 ≈ 101.7 rps — exactly at the 100 rps demand with zero utilization headroom; on the floored 17 whole-context slots, 50 hosts deliver only 98.8 rps.'

quoted_clause: de-escalate when 30-day p95 utilization < 40% AND SLO margin > 2× AND the smaller tier's failure domain is acceptable.
observed: "SLO margin > 2×" is not computable without a denominator. It could mean 2× headroom in latency, 2× utilization margin, or something else.
correction: Define the metric, e.g. "p95 latency ≤ 0.5× SLO" or "SLO headroom > 2× current p95 latency".
acceptance_test: The threshold must be expressible as a measurable inequality.
verdict_evidence: The caption's de-escalation rule reads '30-day p95 utilization < 40% AND SLO margin > 2× AND the smaller tier's failure domain is acceptable' — no quantity is defined for the 2× multiplier (latency headroom? utilization headroom?), and the body never defines it.
fix_instruction: Define the metric in the caption: 'AND SLO headroom ≥ 2× (30-day p95 TTFT ≤ half the SLO) AND ...'.
